title.en: Hariwali and the Faithless Wives
title.zh: 哈里瓦利與不忠之妻

region.zh: 蓋亞那莫魯卡-波默龍阿拉瓦克之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. II 'Tribal Heroes', §§3-4

summary.en: Hariwali, a painstaking piai (medicine-man), spent his days felling timber for his two wives, who took turns carrying him cassiri in the field. One wife was seduced by his brother and broke the calabash, feigning a fall; the shrewd piai knew exactly what had happened. At the pond he bewitched them both: the faithless one cried 'hard to break' as she split wood and flew away as a hawk, while the other bathed and became the first porpoise ever to swim in those waters.
summary.zh: 醫師哈里瓦利終日伐木為二妻耕田，二妻輪流送酒。其一為夫弟所誘，破甕裝傷；智者心中瞭然。於池畔施術：不貞者呼『難碎』而化鷹飛去，另一入池化作海豚——此乃此地第一頭海豚。

sensitivity.note: Guiana Arawak oral tradition recorded by W. E. Roth in 1915 from colonial-era informants; archival record of a living tradition, presented critically and without claiming consent for the communities concerned.

passages.text: Hariwali was a clever, painstaking piai who spent most of his time clearing the field for his two wives. While he felled the timber, the wives undertook, turn and turn about, to bring their husband some cassiri daily. One day, as the wife carried the usual refreshment, the brother-in-law met her, bringing itiriti strands to weave baskets with. 'Do you like me?' he asked. She tempted him sorely, threw her arms round him, and he was but mortal. Before she reached the field she broke the calabash and cut her knee with a pointed stick to make it bleed.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §3; not verbatim.

passages.text: Hariwali saw her come limping with the broken calabash and heard her tale of a fall on a stump. He was a shrewd piai and knew exactly what had happened. Next morning he bade both women cook at the pond; a turtle that they thought they had killed crawled off the hot pot twice — the omen betokening their death, for he had bewitched them. As the faithless wife broke up firewood she exclaimed 'Tata — Ketaiaba — hard to break'; no sooner were the words out of her mouth than she flew away as a hawk. The other, bathing in the pond, became the very first porpoise ever to swim in those waters.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §4; not verbatim.

title.en: Hariwali Rescues His Brother and Rides the Wonderful Tree
title.zh: 哈里瓦利救弟與神樹升天

region.zh: 蓋亞那莫魯卡-波默龍阿拉瓦克之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. II 'Tribal Heroes', §§5-8

summary.en: The brother Hariwali had ruined at hunting found himself trapped on an island, was carried to a spirit's house where the Yawahu removed all his bones but those of his fingers and let spirit children sharpen their arrows on his bony tips. Hariwali, softened at last, played the rattle, had a seed thrown down by parrots, and planted a wonderful tree. He freed his brother, restored his bones, and escaped by changing a probing stick into a bush-master snake; then the whole family climbed the tree, which uprooted itself and flew into the sky — all but the sister who went back for her forgotten apron and was left on earth as a whistling duck.
summary.zh: 弟靈被困於鬼屋，被取盡骨而留指骨，鬼童以之磨箭。哈里瓦利召鸚鵡擲種，種出神樹；救弟歸，以蛇化棍阻鬼。全家登樹，樹自拔而飛天——惟姊返取圍裙，留於人間，化為鳴鴨。

sensitivity.note: Guiana Arawak oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Hariwali's brother could hit nothing now, until a bird told him to look behind: there lay a sheet of water — he was on an island. Round and round he wandered until he found not an ordinary path but a Yawahu's path leading to the Spirit's house. The Yawahu caught him and took all his bones except those of his fingers, tied the bones in a bundle under the roof, and laid him in a hammock, where his spirit children sharpened their blunted arrows on the captive's bony fingertips. In his own house Hariwali's mother wept every night for her absent son.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §§5; not verbatim.

passages.text: Softened at last, Hariwali called up his spirit friends with the rattle, asked the passing parrots to throw down a seed, and planted it where it fell: by next morning a stately tree had grown. He freed his brother and untied the bones from the roof, but the returning Yawahu put dogs on their scent; the two crawled into an armadillo hole, and when the spirit shoved a stick in, Hariwali touched it and changed it into a bush-master snake. The bones were packed back into their brother's skin, and the two made their way home.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §§6-7; not verbatim.

passages.text: The mother had packed everything among the branches of the wonderful tree. As night fell, big and little climbed into the lower branches while Hariwali climbed to the summit and played the shak-shak till midnight. Then the tree shook, rumbled, was rooted out of the sand and began to fly up into the air. But the piai's sister, feeling chilly, remembered her apron left behind and cried 'Deheweyo-daiba — my apron back!' Slipping down to fetch it, she was changed into a wicsai-duck that still whistles those two words. The tree flew away with the rest of the family, and nothing more has been heard of them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §8; not verbatim.

title.en: Haburi's Father and the Tiger in Disguise
title.zh: 哈布里的父親與虎之偽形

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. II 'Tribal Heroes', §§9-11

summary.en: Two childless sisters found that someone was preparing the starch of the ite palm they had cut; watching by night, they begged a manicole-palm leaf to become a man. It did: Mayara-koto. The elder sister bore Haburi. Mayara-koto fished in Tiger's pond and was killed; Tiger took his shape and voice and came home with the stolen fish, snoring and calling his own name, until the sisters heard the fraud, slipped a bark bundle into his arms in place of the baby, and fled with Haburi.
summary.zh: 二姊妹夜守棕櫚，請葉化人，名瑪雅拉科托；長姊生哈布里。瑪雅拉科托捕虎魚而被殺；虎化其形攜魚歸家，鼾聲呼己名；二姊識破，以樹皮束代嬰兒，攜哈布里逃走。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Long ago two sisters minded themselves, with no man to look after them. They cut down an ite tree to manufacture flour, and found the starch lying there ready prepared, again and again. Watching by night, they saw a leaf of the neighboring manicole palm bend over and over until it touched the cut trunk of the ite palm. Both sisters rushed up and caught hold of it, begging it earnestly to turn into a man. It refused at first, but as they begged so earnestly it did so. His name was Mayara-koto. The big elder sister was happy now, and by-and-by she had a beautiful baby boy, called Haburi.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §9; not verbatim.

passages.text: Mayara-koto was told not to fish in Tiger's pond, but 'Tiger's has plenty. I am going to fish in his.' Tiger came and killed him for stealing his fish, then took Mayara-koto's shape and form and returned to the camp with his basket of fish. The women wondered at the coarse, rough voice. He lay down and snored so loudly he could be heard across the river, and while snoring he called his own name — Mayara-koto. The sisters stopped eating, saying 'This man could not possibly be our husband.' Making a bundle of bark, they slipped it under the sleeping child in his arms, and made off with Haburi while the Tiger-man snored on.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §§10-11; not verbatim.

title.en: Wau-uta and the Silk-Cotton Boat
title.zh: 瓦烏塔與木棉小舟

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. II 'Tribal Heroes', §§11-18

summary.en: Old Wau-uta, a piai woman, sheltered the fleeing sisters and secretly made baby Haburi a youth overnight so she might have him for a lover; she taught him to give her the big birds and foul the small ones for his mother. But the water-dogs revealed the truth. Haburi made boat after boat of wax, clay and different woods — each stolen by a different duck, until one of silk-cotton wood was safe: the first boat, which taught ducks to float. When Wau-uta clung to the gunwale, the brothers battered her fingers with paddles, cut a hollow tree, and sealed her inside the trunk — the tree-frog still cries for her lost lover.
summary.zh: 巫婦瓦烏塔藏二姊妹，夜內令哈布里長成，欲占為情人；水犬揭示真情。哈布里以蠟、泥、各木造舟，屢為鴨竊去；至木棉舟方成——首舟也，鴨因之浮水。瓦烏塔緊抱船舷，槳擊其指；遂困於空心樹中，今之樹蛙猶哭其失愛人。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Wau-uta lied to Tiger and killed him in the thorn-covered doorway, then sent the grieving sisters to the field for cassava, keeping Haburi behind. She made the child grow all at once into a youth and gave him the hairi-hairi flute and arrows. Old Wau-uta desired to make Haburi her lover. She directed him to give her all the big birds he shot, and his mother and aunt only the little ones, fouled first — to vex the sisters into leaving. The two sisters would not go; they kept searching the neighborhood for their little child.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §§11-13; not verbatim.

passages.text: Haburi missed a bird at last, his arrow sticking over a creek where his uncles the water-dogs fed. They scented the air — 'That worthless nephew of ours, Haburi' — and told him the old woman was not his mother; it was very wicked to divide the birds so unfairly, and in future he must do exactly the opposite. Haburi carried out their instructions, and when Wau-uta heard it she seized him by the neck, blew into his face, and nagged him all day and night. He resolved to get away, and with his mother and aunt arranged to flee by water.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §§13-15; not verbatim.

passages.text: He made a corial of beeswax; a black duck stole it. One of clay; another duck took it. Boat after boat of varying wood — each stolen by a different species of duck — until one made of silk-cotton tree was not stolen. It was thus Haburi who first made a boat and taught the ducks to float on the water, for each duck has its own particular kind of boat. When Wau-uta clung to the gunwale crying 'My son! I am your mother,' they struck her fingers with their paddles, then cut a hollow tree full of bees and shut her inside. There she is to this day — the Wau-uta frog heard only in hollow trees, still crying for her lost lover.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §§15-17; not verbatim.

title.en: Kororomanna and the Drum of the Dead Baboon
title.zh: 科羅羅瑪納與死狒狒之鼓聲

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. II 'Tribal Heroes', §§19-21

summary.en: Kororomanna, creator of mankind's male half, lost his way home at nightfall with a baboon he had shot, camped on a Hebu (spirit) road, and kept the swelling carcass beside him lest the Hebus steal it. Wakened by the spirits knocking on trees, he struck the carcass in mimicry, and it boomed like a drum. The frightened Hebu begged for a posterior that would let him make such a sound; Kororomanna split the spirit with his bow and impaled him, so that the spirit cursed him and summoned the other Hebus to avenge his death.
summary.zh: 科羅羅瑪納射得狒狒而迷路，夜宿鬼道旁，抱屍而眠；鬼擊樹聲醒之，學而擊屍，隆隆如鼓。鬼驚求為其後竅，俾能作此聲；乃以弓剖之而殺。鬼臨死咒之，召群鬼復仇。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Kororomanna went out hunting and shot a baboon, but it was late in the afternoon, and trying to make his way home he lost his way in the darkness. He made his benab and lay down with the baboon beside him — for where he lay was a Hebu road, along which the tree-dwelling Hebus were always knocking branches and trunks with short sharp crackling noises. Lest the Hebus steal the carcass as it swelled with noxious humors, he kept it alongside and watched over it with a stick. At last he fell asleep; in the middle of the night the Hebus knocked him awake.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §19; not verbatim.

passages.text: He mimicked the Spirits blow for blow: as they struck a limb of a tree, Kororomanna would strike the belly of the baboon, and with each blow there came a resonant Boom! Boom! just like the beating of a drum. The Hebu leader was frightened, begged Kororomanna to make for him a posterior which would allow of his producing a similar sound, for he and all his family had none, only a red spot. With his bow Kororomanna split the Spirit's hindquarters and completed the task by impaling him, piercing him even to the head. The Hebu cursed him, threatened that the other Spirits would avenge his death, and disappeared.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §§20-21; not verbatim.

title.en: The Hebus Lay Siege to the Manicole Tree
title.zh: 群鬼圍攻馬尼科爾樹

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. II 'Tribal Heroes', §§22-23

summary.en: When the Hebus came to avenge their dead, Kororomanna climbed the manicole tree over his shelter, leaving the baboon's body to be beaten as if it were himself. Their axes were water-turtle shells, their knives seed-pods; their rope was a snake, whose head he cut off. A spirit climbed head-downward — for the Hebus can look upward only upside-down — and was killed with the same blow; then Kororomanna hurled the body down shouting the preconcerted signal, and the Hebus clubbed one of their own to pieces while he slipped away into the bush.
summary.zh: 群鬼復仇而至；科羅羅瑪納登樹而留屍代己。鬼斧乃龜殼，刀乃果莢，繩乃蛇——其首被斬。一鬼倒懸爬樹，被殺；瑪納呼預定暗號擲屍，群鬼誤擊同類；而彼滑落遁入林中。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Swarms of Hebus approached the scene of the outrage, so Kororomanna climbed the manicole tree sheltering his benab, leaving the baboon's corpse inside. The Spirits entered, believed the dead animal to be Kororomanna, and began hitting it — and with each blow there came the Boom! of the swollen carcass. Up in the tree he could not help laughing, and one of the spirits, standing on his head — for the Hebus, with their great eyebrows, can look upward only in this upside-down position — peeped up and saw him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §22; not verbatim.

passages.text: They decided to hew down the tree, but their axes were water-turtle shells and their knives only seed-pods of the buari tree, which broke; the rope they fetched was a snake, and as it came within reach Kororomanna cut its head off. One great spirit was chosen to climb and throw him down, shouting the signal Tura-buna-at mahara-ko na-hai. Climbing head-downward, he was killed by the same peculiar blow as the first; then Kororomanna hurled the dead body down with the cry of the signal, and the Hebus below clubbed one of their own to pieces. He slipped down, helped in the dissolution, told them he would 'soon return' — and vanished into the bush.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §23; not verbatim.

title.en: Kororomanna and the Snake's Wife
title.zh: 科羅羅瑪納與蛇之妻

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. II 'Tribal Heroes', §§25-26

summary.en: Still lost, Kororomanna sheltered in a hollow tree where a woman warned him that her husband Snake would smell him out. When Snake came he listed the avenging relatives — a hummingbird uncle, a doroquaira, a chicken-hawk — and the serpent, afraid of the hawk above all, let him go. Trapped later in a spring-trap set by Hebus, he fouled himself and lay as if dead; carried to the river as a stinking 'fish', he rolled away into the water while the spirits went to plait a basket for his flesh.
summary.zh: 瑪納避於空心樹，蛇夫將至；因言獵鷹復仇，蛇懼而縱之。後陷於鬼設彈簧魚簍，詐死；鬼運至河邊欲剖洗，趁其取藤結籃，滾入水中而脫。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: In a hollow tree Kororomanna found a woman, and told her he would remain till 'the day cleaned'. She warned him that her man was Snake, who would be back before dawn and would certainly kill him. Before daybreak Snake came wending home, crying that he could smell someone. Our hero named his uncles: a hummingbird, a doroquaira, then a chicken-hawk flying along — 'and when I am dead, he also will come and search for me.' Snake feared the hawk, which used always to get the better of him; so he let Kororomanna go in peace, and the man ran out pretty quick.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §§25-26; not verbatim.

passages.text: He came on a clean roadway and his foot stuck in it like a fish in a spring-trap — a trap set by the Hebus. He fouled himself over completely and lay quite still, pretending to be dead, while flies gathered and were followed by worms. Two Spirits came along: 'My spring-trap has caught a fish at last' — 'Oh! I have left it too long. It stinks.' They carried it to the riverside to wash and clean it, and agreed to make a waiyarri basket first, to put the flesh in. While they collected strands to plait with, Kororomanna rolled down the river bank into the water and made good his escape.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §25; not verbatim.

title.en: Kororomanna and the Footprint Curse
title.zh: 科羅羅瑪納與足印之咒

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. II 'Tribal Heroes', §§26-27

summary.en: Finding a Hebu's baby in a fallen hollow tree, Kororomanna slaughtered it and climbed away as the mother came. She dug up a bit of his footprint, wrapped it in a leaf, and cursed over the fire to draw his shadow into the flames; but he had swapped the parcel for one of her own footprints. Twice she was dragged toward the fire against her will; the third time she fell in and was burnt to ashes. Later he planted an arrow in a Hebu skull's eye and was forced to carry the skull, which pursued him and drowned in a creek.
summary.zh: 瑪納殺鬼嬰，登樹而藏。鬼母掘其足印裹咒火燒，欲引其影入火；然彼已換以鬼母足印。母三被火拖曳，終墮火焚為灰。後其以箭刺鬼骷髏之目，被迫負之而行，骷髏終追之落水而亡。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Inside a fallen hollow tree across his path Kororomanna saw a baby — a Hebu's child — and slaughtered it, climbing a neighboring tree as the footsteps of the mother came near. She recognized her dead infant, examined the fresh tracks, dug up the soil marked by one of the footprints, wrapped it in a leaf tied with bush-rope, and hung it on a branch while she went for firewood.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §26; not verbatim.

passages.text: Her back was hardly turned before Kororomanna substituted a footprint of the Spirit woman. When she returned she made a big fire, threw the bundle into the flames, and cursed: 'May the owner of this footprint fall into this fire also!' — thinking the shadow would be drawn to the fire. No one came, and she felt her own shadow impelled. 'It seems that I am hurting myself,' she exclaimed. Twice she was thus dragged toward the fire against her will; on the third occasion she could not draw back — she fell in and was burnt to ashes.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §26; not verbatim.

passages.text: Next he jerked his arrow into the eye of a man's skull lying on the ground — a Hebu called Kwa-muhu, who cried: 'Now you have injured me, you will have to carry me.' Kororomanna carried and fed the skull on a bark-strip until it grew a dead weight; he set it down, ran to a creek, and swam across. The skull, pursuing him, mistook a running deer for his man and killed it at the water's edge, then counted two fingers — 'But the man I am after had five fingers and a long nose. You must be somebody else.' Enraged, it tried to leap the creek, but having no legs it fell into the water and was drowned.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §27; not verbatim.

title.en: Kororomanna and the Bundle of Fish
title.zh: 科羅羅瑪納與魚之束

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. II 'Tribal Heroes', §§27-28

summary.en: Still finding no way home, Kororomanna met the Hebu Huta-Kurakura bailing a pond with his own huge scrotum; he shot him twice in the back before being hurled into timber with only his eye left projecting. He ransomed himself with tobacco, the two emptied the pond of fish, and the spirit bound the whole catch into one small bundle. Every animal he met on the way home had been begging food from his mother; when his family opened the little parcel, fish after fish filled the whole house and drove its occupants outside.
summary.zh: 瑪納遇鬼赫塔庫拉庫拉以其陰囊舀水；射之，被擲入木中。以菸草贖身，共舀乾池而得魚；鬼以奇法束之成小包。沿途諸獸皆言向其母乞食；歸家開包，魚不可勝數，滿屋而出。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Kororomanna came upon an old man bailing water out of a pond — really the Hebu Huta-Kurakura, Red-back, anxious for the fish, having no calabash he bailed with his very large purse [scrotum]. Not knowing what sort of creature it was, Kororomanna stuck him twice in the back; the spirit only slapped the spot as at a cow-fly, but on the third arrow turned, seized the wanderer, and hurled him into a piece of wood with such force that only his eye projected from the timber. He offered crystals, rattles, paiwarri, women; only tobacco was eagerly accepted, and they fast became good friends.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §27; not verbatim.

passages.text: They both emptied the pond and collected a heap of fish much too large to carry home. The Spirit in some peculiar way bound them all into quite a small bundle, small enough for Kororomanna to carry in his hand. Every animal on the homeward road gave him news of his mother — a rat with a potato, an acouri with cassava root, a labba with a yam, a bush-cow eating a pineapple: each said 'I have been to your mother, and have begged things from her.' At home his wife and mother laughed at his claim of many fish — till they opened the parcel and out came fish after fish, small and large, until the house was filled and the occupants had to shift outside.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §28; not verbatim.

title.en: Nahakoboni Carves a Daughter: the Sun Comes Courting
title.zh: 納哈科博尼雕女與日神求婚

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. II 'Tribal Heroes', §§29-31

summary.en: Old Nahakoboni, 'he who eats plenty', had no daughter and no son-in-law for his declining years, so he carved a lovely woman, Usidiu, from a plum tree. Birds and beasts came courting and were refused; but Yar the Sun himself came, and the old man tested him — devouring his barbecue, making him fetch water with a leaking quake (a Hebu sealed it), haul a sunken corial, and shoot fish without looking into the water, an alligator becoming the bench and a snake the fish-arrow. Satisfied, Nahakoboni gave him the plum-tree daughter.
summary.zh: 納哈科博尼無女無婿，刻李木為女，名烏西迪烏。鳥獸求婚皆拒；日神雅爾至。老人試之：食其炙肉，令以漏籃取水（鬼助之）、撈沉舟、望天射魚；鱷化凳、蛇化箭。乃以雕女妻之。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically. The wood-carved woman parallels human-molding motifs elsewhere; tagged accordingly as an interpretive choice.

passages.text: Nahakoboni, the one who eats plenty, was an old man who, never having had a daughter, felt anxious about his declining years, for he had no son-in-law to care for him. He therefore carved a daughter for himself out of a plum tree, and being a medicine-man cut and carved the timber so skilfully that there was indeed a woman lovely to gaze upon. Her name was Usidiu — seed-tree. All the animals, bird and beast, came from far to court her, but the old man liked none of them and gave them all a curt refusal.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §29; not verbatim.

passages.text: When Yar, the Sun himself, stopped on his journey to pay court, Nahakoboni tested him: he ate heartily of Yar's barbecue, then demanded drink, then water to bathe with — but the quake Yar dipped always leaked, until a Hebu made the water stay. Yar hauled up the sunken corial at the waterside; where the bench should be under a tree's roots an alligator crouched, and seized by the neck it changed into a bench; a big snake became the fish-arrow. 'Shoot up into the air, and do not look into the water,' said the old man; the arrow pierced and killed the great kwabaihi fish. Thoroughly satisfied, Nahakoboni gave him his plum-tree daughter.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §§30-31; not verbatim.

title.en: The Spiteful Father-in-law: Fields That Regrew Overnight
title.zh: 忿怒之岳父：夜復生之田

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. II 'Tribal Heroes', §§32-33

summary.en: Angry with Yar the Sun for complaining of his carved daughter, Nahakoboni bided his time. By his medicine the field Yar cut regrew overnight, lush as ever, so the Sun cut it twice more in vain; the third time his Hebu friend pulled out the stumps for him, and Nahakoboni planted cassava and plantains — and ripened them overnight too. Still unsatisfied, he pulled down the house Yar built and made him rebuild it of the hardest purple-heart; then took charge of it and lived there.
summary.zh: 老人怒日神嫌其雕女，待機報復；以術令已伐之田夜復葱蘢，日神三伐無效。鬼友拔其樁，老人播木薯香蕉，夜熟其穀；又毀日神所築之屋，令改以紫心木重築，遂占居之。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Although the old man evinced no ill-will, he was greatly displeased with his son-in-law — for complaining of the piece of sculpture, and for allowing the bunia bird to 'tinker' with it. He bided his time until Yar undertook the customary marriage task of cutting a field. Yar worked early and late, and told his wife the field was ready for inspection; but on returning home Nahakoboni found fault, for by his medicine he had made all the trees and bushes regrow overnight, as luxuriant as before. Yar cut another and a bigger field, and just the same thing happened.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §32; not verbatim.

passages.text: A third field was cut; Yar tried to pull out the stumps by the roots and could not shift one, falling down exhausted. His old friend the Hebu put in an appearance, did the job for him, and advised him home. Nahakoboni came to inspect, planted cassava, plantains and other useful plants, and returned in the evening without a word — next morning there stood a beautiful crop of ripe cassava and plantains. So when his son-in-law completed the other marriage task, the building of a house, the old man pulled it down and said he wanted it built stronger; Yar rebuilt it of purple-heart, the hardest timber he could find, and Nahakoboni, pleased at last, took charge of the house and lived there.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §§32-33; not verbatim.

title.en: The Unborn Twins Guide Their Mother to the Frog's House
title.zh: 未生雙子引母至蛙婦之屋

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. II 'Tribal Heroes', §§33

summary.en: Yar the Sun went west and told his pregnant wife Usidiu to follow the right-hand track, marked by scattered feathers, to his distant house. Where the wind had blown the feathers away her unborn child spoke and guided her, and told her to pluck the pretty flowers — until a marabunta wasp stung her, she struck at it and missed, and the babe, misreading the smack, refused any longer to guide her. Lost and weary, she reached the house of Nanyobo, the great old frog-woman, was told to pick the insects from the old woman's head — and, overcome with fatigue, put a louse between her teeth and fell dead.
summary.zh: 日神西行，令孕妻循右手之路，沿途撒羽為記。風吹羽失，未生之子開口引路，囑摘路花；胡蜂螫之，母拍未中，子誤為責己，怒而不言。母迷失至大蛙婦南約博之屋，為其拾蝨，疲倦忘戒，以蝨入口，遂死。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Yar, the Sun, told his wife he proposed taking a journey to the westward, but that as she was now pregnant she had better travel at her leisure: he would start first and she must follow his tracks, always taking the right-hand track, for he would scatter feathers on the left so that she could make no mistake. She avoided the feathers till she reached a spot where the wind had blown them away, and then the trouble began. Her very motherhood proved her salvation, because her unborn babe began talking and told her which path to follow.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §33; not verbatim.

passages.text: The child told her to pluck the pretty flowers bobbing over the roadway; she had picked some when a marabunta wasp stung her below the waist, and in trying to kill it she missed and struck herself. The unborn baby, misinterpreting her action as a smack, became vexed and refused any longer to show her the direction. Hopelessly astray, more dead than alive, she found herself before a very large house whose only occupant was Nanyobo, a very old and very big frog-woman. She was told to clean her hostess's head, 'but mind, do not put the insects into your mouth, because they will poison you.' Overcome with fatigue and anxiety, she forgot the injunction, picked out a louse, placed it between her teeth as is customary — and fell dead.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §33; not verbatim.

title.en: The Twins Discover Fire: Makunaima and Pia Kill the Old Frog
title.zh: 雙子識火：馬庫納伊瑪與皮亞誅老蛙

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. II 'Tribal Heroes', §§34

summary.en: Old Nanyobo slashed open the dead mother and extracted not one child but two — the beautiful boys Makunaima and Pia — and minded them well. She always sent them to dry their fish in the sun, never over a fire, yet fed them cooked fish: she vomited fire from her mouth, cooked, and licked the fire up again. One brother changed himself into a lizard and watched from the roof, seeing her also scratch her neck for balata-milk to make starch. 'What old woman do, no good. Kill old woman.' They tied her to a tree and burned her; the fire passed from her body into the fagots of hima-heru wood — from which we still get fire by rubbing two sticks together.
summary.zh: 老蛙婦剖亡母而取出雙子：馬庫納伊瑪與皮亞。彼令曝魚於日，不許就火，然魚皆已炊熟——原來其口中吐火，炊畢舔滅。其一化蜥登屋窺之，見其搔頸取乳為粉。『老婦所為不善，殺之。』縛於樹而焚；火自其身入柴，此柴即取火之木。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Old Nanyobo thereupon slashed open the mother, and extracted not one child but two — a pair of beautiful boys, Makunaima and Pia. Nanyobo proved a kind foster-mother and minded them well. As the babies grew they commenced shooting birds, then fish and game. On each occasion she would say, 'You must dry your fish in the sun, and never over a fire' — yet by the time they returned with the firewood she had sent for, the fish would be all nicely cooked and ready. As a matter of fact she would vomit fire out of her mouth, do her cooking, and lick the fire up again before the lads' return; she apparently never let them see fire burning.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §34; not verbatim.

passages.text: Day after day made the boys suspicious, and they determined to find out how the old lady made her fire. When next despatched for firewood, one of them changed himself into a lizard, ran back up into the roof, and watched: he saw the old woman vomit out fire, use it, and lick it up again, and also scratch her neck, whence flowed something like balata milk, out of which she prepared starch. Their deliberations were summarized tersely: 'What old woman do, no good. Kill old woman.' They tied her to a fine tree in the middle of a large cleared field and burned her; as she was consumed the fire within her passed into the surrounding fagots of hima-heru wood — the timber from which we still get fire by rubbing two sticks together.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §34; not verbatim.

title.en: Tiger's Mother and the Powis Bird's Revelation
title.zh: 虎母與鳳冠鳥之啟示

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍加勒比之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. II 'Tribal Heroes', §§35-36

summary.en: A woman pregnant by the Sun with twins Pia and Makunaima lost her way after quarrelling with her unborn children and arrived at the house of Tiger's mother, the Rain-frog. The frog hid her in the big cassiri jar, but Tiger smelled her out and killed her, extracting the unborn twins, whom his mother ordered him to cherish in a cotton bundle. They grew to man's size in a month; a Powis bird told them it was Tiger who had killed their mother; they shot him from a staging and slaughtered the old woman too.
summary.zh: 孕於日神之婦與未生雙子失和而迷路，至虎母雨蛙之屋。蛙婦匿之於酒甕，虎聞而殺之，取出雙子；蛙母命以棉束育之。一月而成人形；鳳冠鳥告以其母乃虎所殺；遂於高臺射虎，並誅老婦。

sensitivity.note: Carib oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: A long time ago there was a woman who had become pregnant by the Sun, with twin children, Pia and Makunaima. When she stumbled and hurt herself on the road she blamed her two unborn children as the cause; they became vexed and refused to tell her which road to follow, and thus it was that she took the wrong direction and arrived, foot-sore and weary, at a curious house belonging to Tiger's mother, Kono(bo)-aru, the Rain-frog. The house-mistress took pity on her and hid her in the big cassiri jar, popping on the cover; but Tiger, sniffing up and down, peeped into the jar and discovered the frightened creature.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §35; not verbatim.

passages.text: On killing the poor woman, Tiger found the two as-yet-unborn children, and his mother said he must now mind and cherish them; so he put them in a bundle of cotton to keep them warm, and they crept next day, grew fast, and reached man's size in about a month. Tiger's mother told them to go and shoot the Powis because it was this bird which had killed their own mother. Day after day they shot Powis, until the last bird told them it was none of his tribe but Tiger himself who had killed their mother. The boys went home empty-handed on the excuse that the Powis had taken their arrows — they had hidden the arrows to make new and stronger weapons — built a staging against a tree, shot and killed Tiger as he passed below, and reached home to slaughter his mother also.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §36; not verbatim.

title.en: The Frog's Cassava Shoulder and the Wrinkled Skin
title.zh: 蛙婦之肩粉與皺皮

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍加勒比之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. II 'Tribal Heroes', §§37

summary.en: Travelling on to meet their father the Sun, the twins lodged with a very old woman who was really a frog, in a house among cotton-trees. She always had cassava ready though no field was anywhere about; hiding behind a tree, the boys saw her bend down and pick at a white spot on her shoulders, and observed the cassava-starch fall. They teased out cotton as a soft bed for her; as soon as she sat upon it they set fire to it, scorching her skin so dreadfully as to give it the wrinkled and rough appearance it bears to this day.
summary.zh: 雙子途中宿於棉林間老婦之屋——實蛙也。其無田而常有薯餅；伏樹窺之，見其俯身肩上白斑，薯粉自落。二人採棉為褥，老婦喜而坐之；即縱火焚之，灼其皮，皺縮之狀至今猶然。

sensitivity.note: Carib oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Pia and Makunaima proceeded on their way and arrived at last at a clump of cotton-trees in the center of which was a house occupied by a very old woman, really a frog, with whom they took up their quarters. They went out hunting each day and on their return invariably found some cassava their hostess had baked. 'That's very strange,' remarked Pia to his brother, 'there is no field anywhere about, and yet look at the quantity of cassava. We must watch her.' Next morning they hid themselves behind a tree whence they could see everything that took place at the house.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §37; not verbatim.

passages.text: They noticed that the old frog had a white spot on her shoulders; they saw her bend down and pick at this spot, and observed the cassava-starch fall. On their return home they refused to eat the usual cake, having now discovered its source. Next morning they picked cotton from the neighboring trees and teased it out on the floor, telling her it was something nice and soft for her to lie upon. Much pleased, she promptly sat upon it — and no sooner had she done so than the two lads set fire to it, scorching her skin so dreadfully as to give it the wrinkled and rough appearance it bears to this day.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §37; not verbatim.

title.en: The Tapir, the Severed Leg, and the Stars
title.zh: 貘、斷腿與眾星

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍加勒比之地

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. II 'Tribal Heroes', §38

summary.en: On their way to meet their father the twins spent three days with a Maipuri (tapir) woman, sleek and fat when she returned each evening. Following her tracks to a plum-tree, they shook it so violently that all the fruit, ripe and unripe, fell and lay wasted; the furious tapir beat both boys and fled into the bush. They pursued her for many a long day; Pia told Makunaima to wheel in front and drive her back, but as she passed the harpoon-arrow flew and the rope cut his leg off. On a clear night you can still see them among the clouds: Maipuri the Hyades, Makunaima the Pleiades, and below, his severed leg — Orion's Belt.
summary.zh: 雙子宿貘婦之家三日，見其晚歲肥潤；尋跡至李樹，搖之使果盡落，貘怒而遁。追之累日；皮亞令馬庫納伊瑪迎頭驅之，魚叉疾發，繩索斷其腿。晴夜猶見雲間：貘乃畢宿、雙子乃昴宿、斷腿乃獵戶帶。

sensitivity.note: Carib oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Pia and Makunaima next continued their travels to meet their father, and soon arrived at the house of a Maipuri (tapir), where they spent three days. On the third evening Maipuri returned, looking very sleek and fat. Wanting to know what she had been feeding on, the boys followed her tracks to a plum-tree; this they shook and shook so violently as to make all the fruit, both ripe and unripe, fall to the ground, where it lay wasted. When Maipuri went to feed next morning she was disgusted to see her food thus destroyed, and in a very angry mood quickly returned home, beat both boys, and cleared out into the bush.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §38; not verbatim.

passages.text: The boys started in pursuit, tracked her for many a long day, and at last caught up with her. Pia told Makunaima to wheel round in front and drive the creature back to him, and as she passed he let fly a harpoon-arrow; the rope, however, got in the way of Makunaima as he passed in front, and cut his leg off. On a clear night you can still see them up among the clouds: there is Maipuri (Hyades), there Makunaima (Pleiades), and below is his severed leg (Orion's Belt).
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §38; not verbatim.

title.en: Alligator's Carved Daughter and the Woodpecker
title.zh: 鱷之雕女與啄木鳥

region.zh: 羅賴馬草原馬庫希之地

texts.period: Makusi oral tradition; recorded 1915 (Roth, after Dance)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. II 'Tribal Heroes', §39

summary.en: The Sun's fish-ponds were constantly robbed; Yamimi the water-lizard failed as watchman, and Alligator — the real thief — was detected and slashed with a cutlass, every cut forming a scale. To propitiate the Sun he offered a beautiful daughter he did not have, so he sculptured her from a wild plum tree and exposed her to the Sun's influence; fearing detection he hid in the water peering up, which he has done ever since. The woman was imperfectly formed, but a woodpecker pecked her body into perfection. The Sun deserted her, and grieving, she set out to seek him.
summary.zh: 日神魚池屢遭竊；水蜥守而不力，鱷乃真賊，被斬，每創成鱗。求贖，謂有美女——實無；遂刻李木為女，曝於日光。畏露而行藏於水，昂首窺日，至今如此。其體未完，啄木鳥啄之乃成。日神棄之；婦悲而尋夫。

sensitivity.note: Makusi oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: The Sun, finding his fish-ponds too frequently robbed, set Yamimi, the water-lizard, to watch them. Yamuru was not sufficiently vigilant, so Alligator was appointed watchman. Alligator, the depredator, continued his old trade while employed as a watchman, and at last was detected by the Sun, who slashed him with a cutlass within an inch of his life, every cut forming a scale. Alligator begged piteously for his life, and to propitiate the Sun offered him his beautiful daughter in marriage. But he had no daughter.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §39; not verbatim.

passages.text: He therefore sculptured the form of a woman from a wild plum tree, exposed her to the Sun's influence, and — fearing ultimate detection of the fraud — hid himself in the water, peering at the Sun; and this habit Alligator has continued to the present time. The woman was imperfectly formed, but a woodpecker, in quest of food, pecked at her body and prepared her. The Sun left her, and she, grieving for his desertion, said that she would seek him — and so came at last to old Mother Toad's house, where she died from the poisonous head-lice, leaving the two unborn children who were to become the twin Heroes.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §39; not verbatim.

title.en: Crane and the Making of Fire; the First Canoe
title.zh: 鶴教取火與首舟

region.zh: 羅賴馬草原馬庫希之地

texts.period: Makusi oral tradition; recorded 1915 (Roth, after Dance)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. II 'Tribal Heroes', §40

summary.en: Pia slew Tiger and took from the carcass the parts of his mother's body, and she became whole and alive. But Makunaima ate live coals, and the toad remonstrated in anger. Makunaima dug a great canal and made a corial — the first of its kind — persuading his mother and Pia to travel with him. From Crane, who struck his bill against a flint so that the friction produced fire, the brothers learned the art of fire-making. They placed huge rocks in all the rivers to detain the fishes — and these rocks caused the great waterfalls. When Crane quarrelled with Pia and flew off with Makunaima to Spanish Guiana, the family was divided forever.
summary.zh: 皮亞誅虎，自其屍取母體之部，母復活。馬庫納伊瑪好吞火炭，蟾母勸之而怒。乃鑿巨渠，造首舟，攜母與兄同行。兄弟自鶴學取火：鶴喙擊石生火。置巨石於諸河以留魚——瀑布由此而生。鶴與皮亞爭，攜馬庫納伊瑪飛往西班牙圭亞那，一家遂散。

sensitivity.note: Makusi oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Pia's first work was to slay Tiger and take out of his carcass the parts of the body of his mother, who became whole and alive. But Makunaima had an appetite for fire-eating, and invariably devoured the live coals. The toad remonstrated, and Makunaima in anger prepared to leave and to travel throughout the land. To attain his purpose he dug a large canal, into which flowed water; and having made a corial — the first of its kind — he persuaded his mother and Pia to go with him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §40; not verbatim.

passages.text: It was from Crane that the brothers learned the art of fire-making, when he struck his bill against a flint and the friction produced fire. The brothers placed huge rocks in all the rivers to detain the fishes: the rocks thus placed caused the great waterfalls. Crane was at first accustomed to catch his own fish, but finding Pia and Makunaima more successful fishermen after the rivers had been dammed, kept near to them and took away their fish. Pia consequently quarrelled with Crane, who, becoming angry, took up Makunaima — who had taken part with him against his brother — and flew away with him to Spanish Guiana.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §40; not verbatim.

title.en: Pia on Roraima: the Mother's Tears Become Streams
title.zh: 皮亞居羅賴馬：母淚成川

region.zh: 圭亞那-巴西-委內瑞拉交界羅賴馬山（馬庫希）

texts.period: Makusi oral tradition; recorded 1915 (Roth, after Dance)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. II 'Tribal Heroes', §§41-42

summary.en: Deserted with his mother, Pia abandoned the hunt and traveled from place to place teaching the Indians many useful and good things — by him and his teachings we have the piai men. He bore his weary mother to the heights of Roraima to be her abiding place of rest. When his time of departure arrived he told her that whatever of good she desired she would obtain if she bowed her head and covered her face with her hands while expressing her wish. Whenever the mother of the twin heroes is sorrowful, a storm rises on the mountain, and it is her tears that run down in streams from the heights of Roraima.
summary.zh: 皮亞與母被棄，乃棄獵而遍行教人善事——醫師之職由之而起。攜疲母登羅賴馬山而安之。臨別囑其俯首掩面而祈，所願必得。雙子之母每悲，山即起風暴；羅賴馬之川，皆其淚也。

sensitivity.note: Makusi oral tradition recorded 1915 (Roth); archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Pia and his mother, thus deserted, continued their daily employment of traveling together, fishing, and seeking fruits. At last one day the mother complained of weariness, and Pia conveyed her to the heights of Roraima, these to be her abiding place of rest. Then came a change of occupation for Pia: he abandoned the hunt as the principal occupation of his life, and traveled from place to place, teaching the Indians many useful and good things. By him and his teachings we have the piai men.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §41; not verbatim.

passages.text: When his time of departure from her had arrived, he told her that whatever of good she desired she would obtain if she would bow her head and cover her face with her hands while she expressed her wish. This she does in her need to the present hour. Whenever the mother of these two heroes of our race is sorrowful, there arises a storm on the mountain, and it is her tears that run down in streams from the heights of Roraima. On Mount Zabang, the Olympus of the Makusis, dwells their great Spirit Makunaima.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §41-42; not verbatim.

title.en: Amalivaca and Vochi Carve the Orinoco
title.zh: 阿馬利瓦卡與沃希鑿奧里諾科

region.zh: 委內瑞拉奧里諾科灘區塔馬納克之地

texts.period: Tamanac tradition recorded by Humboldt; summarized 1915 (Roth)

source.work: Walter E. Roth, An Inquiry into the Animism and Folk-lore of the Guiana Indians (33rd Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1915), ch. II 'Tribal Heroes', §43

summary.en: Amalivaca, venerated by the Caribs and especially the Tamanacs, arrived in a bark during the subsidence of the great waters, and carved the sculptures still seen high on the perpendicular rock faces that border the great rivers. With his brother Vochi he created the world, and while making the Orinoco the two held a long consultation about making the stream flow up and down at one and the same time, to ease the paddlers. Fond of gadding, his daughters were condemned by him to sedentary life — their legs broken to force them to people the land of the Tamanacs. His stone house may still be seen on the plains of Maita, with a great stone beside it said to be 'the drum of Amalivaca'.
summary.zh: 阿馬利瓦卡於大水退時乘舟而至，鑿巨石為紋，至今猶存。與弟沃希共造世界；鑿奧里諾科河時，欲使水上下同流以利舟人。其女好遊，遂折其足使居塔馬納克之地而繁衍。邁塔平原猶見其石屋，旁有大石，號『阿馬利瓦卡之鼓』。

sensitivity.note: Tamanac tradition recorded by Humboldt and summarized in Roth 1915; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Amalivaca, venerated by the Caribs and more especially by the Tamanacs, is said to have arrived in a bark during the subsidence of the great waters, and to have carved the sculptures now seen high on the perpendicular faces of the rocks which border the great rivers. He has a brother, Vochi; together they created the world. While making the Orinoco they had a long consultation about causing the stream to flow up and down at one and the same time, so as to ease the paddlers as much as possible.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §43 (from Humboldt); not verbatim.

passages.text: Amalivaca had daughters who were very fond of gadding about, so he broke their legs to render them sedentary and force them to people the land of the Tamanacs. He also made the earth sufficiently level for people to dwell on, and he seems to have known music. His house, consisting of blocks of stone piled one on another and forming a sort of cavern, may still be seen on the plains of Maita; and near it is a large stone which the Indians say was an instrument of music — 'the drum of Amalivaca'.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Roth 1915, §43 (from Humboldt); not verbatim.
